summary.text: Take \(k=31\), \(s=1\), and the distinct positive integers \(5\) and \(1829=31\cdot59\). Their divisor sums coincide: \(1/32+1/36=17/288\), while \(1/32+1/62+1/90+1/1860=17/288\), so their fractional parts are equal and pairwise distinctness fails.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
S_{k,s}(n)=\sum_{d\mid n}\frac{1}{(d+k)^s}
\]
for positive integers \(n,k,s\), where the sum ranges over the positive divisors of \(n\). We disprove the conjecture by taking
\[
k=31,\qquad s=1
\]
and exhibiting two distinct positive integers with equal sums (and hence equal fractional parts).

Take the two indices
\[
n_1=5,\qquad n_2=1829.
\]
They are plainly positive and distinct.

First consider \(n_1=5\). Since \(5\) is prime, its positive divisors are exactly \(1\) and \(5\). Therefore
\[
\begin{aligned}
S_{31,1}(5)
 &=\frac1{1+31}+\frac1{5+31}\\
 &=\frac1{32}+\frac1{36}\\
 &=\frac9{288}+\frac8{288}\\
 &=\frac{17}{288}.
\end{aligned}
\]

We next determine the positive divisors of \(1829\). There is the factorization
\[
1829=31\cdot 59.
\]
Both factors are prime. For \(31\), it is enough to test the primes not exceeding \(\sqrt{31}<6\), namely \(2,3,5\), and none divides \(31\). For \(59\), it is enough to test \(2,3,5,7\), since \(\sqrt{59}<8\); none divides \(59\) (in particular, \(59\equiv3\pmod 7\)). The primes \(31\) and \(59\) are distinct. Thus, by unique prime factorization, every positive divisor of \(1829=31^1 59^1\) has the form \(31^a59^b\) with \(a,b\in\{0,1\}\). Consequently its positive divisors are exactly
\[
1,\ 31,\ 59,\ 1829.
\]
It follows that
\[
\begin{aligned}
S_{31,1}(1829)
 &=\frac1{1+31}+\frac1{31+31}
   +\frac1{59+31}+\frac1{1829+31}\\
 &=\frac1{32}+\frac1{62}+\frac1{90}+\frac1{1860}.
\end{aligned}
\]
To evaluate this sum, use the common denominator \(44640\). Indeed,
\[
\frac{44640}{32}=1395,\qquad
\frac{44640}{62}=720,\qquad
\frac{44640}{90}=496,\qquad
\frac{44640}{1860}=24.
\]
Hence
\[
\begin{aligned}
S_{31,1}(1829)
 &=\frac{1395+720+496+24}{44640}\\
 &=\frac{2635}{44640}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Both numerator and denominator are divisible by \(155=5\cdot31\), and
\[
2635=155\cdot17,\qquad 44640=155\cdot288.
\]
Therefore
\[
S_{31,1}(1829)=\frac{17}{288}.
\]
Combining the two calculations gives
\[
S_{31,1}(5)=S_{31,1}(1829)=\frac{17}{288}.
\]
In particular, their fractional parts are equal. More explicitly, since
\(0<17/288<1\), each fractional part is itself \(17/288\):
\[
\operatorname{frac}(S_{31,1}(5))
 =\frac{17}{288}
 =\operatorname{frac}(S_{31,1}(1829)).
\]

The conjecture asserts its two conclusions for every positive pair \((k,s)\). In particular, at the positive pair \((31,1)\), its pairwise-distinctness conclusion would say that equality of these fractional parts forces the corresponding positive indices to be equal. Applied to \(n_1=5\) and \(n_2=1829\), it would therefore force
\[
5=1829,
\]
which is false.

Thus the pairwise-distinctness part of the conjecture fails for \(k=31\) and \(s=1\). Since the original statement is universal in \(k\) and \(s\) and is a conjunction containing this pairwise-distinctness assertion, this single counterexample disproves the entire conjecture. (The separate claim that none of the sums is an integer is not needed for the contradiction; indeed, the common value \(17/288\) in this example is nonintegral.)
